rows.question: Is place-based predictive policing prohibited under the AI Act?
rows.answer: No. Article 5(1)(d) only prohibits AI systems that assess or predict the risk that an individual natural person will commit a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on assessing their personality traits and characteristics. Place-based predictive policing forecasts where crime is likely to occur rather than assessing individuals, so it falls outside that prohibition. It is also not a listed Annex III(6) law-enforcement use case, because those points cover assessments of natural persons. That changes if the system profiles or risk-scores identifiable individuals, which would bring it back toward Article 5(1)(d) or the Annex III(6) high-risk category.

rows.question: Is predictive policing prohibited under the AI Act?
rows.answer: Predictive policing is not always prohibited. Article 5(1)(d) prohibits AI systems that assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling of that person or on assessing their personality traits and characteristics. That prohibition does not apply to AI systems that support a human assessment of a person's involvement in a criminal activity, where that assessment is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to the activity. Predictive tools outside the ban are high-risk under Annex III(6)(d) when law enforcement authorities use them to assess a natural person's risk of offending or re-offending other than solely on the basis of profiling, or to assess personality traits or past criminal behaviour.

rows.question: If place-based predictive policing tools (forecasting where crime will happen rather than who will commit it) prove harmful, could the Commission bring them into Annex III by delegated act, and what has to happen before such an act takes effect?
rows.answer: Yes, but only within the limits Article 7 sets. Under Article 7(1) the Commission may adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 to amend Annex III by adding or modifying use cases of high-risk AI systems where both of the following conditions are fulfilled: the AI systems are intended to be used in any of the areas already listed in Annex III, and they pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, that is equivalent to or greater than the risk of harm or adverse impact posed by the high-risk AI systems already referred to in Annex III. Both conditions are cumulative, so a use case outside the existing areas cannot be added by delegated act; Article 7(2) lists the criteria for assessing that risk, and Article 7(3) allows a use case to be removed from Annex III where it no longer poses a significant risk and the overall level of protection is not reduced. Before adopting the delegated act the Commission must consult experts designated by each Member State (Article 97(4)), and the act enters into force only if neither the European Parliament nor the Council objects within three months of notification, a period extended by three months at the initiative of either of them, or earlier where both inform the Commission that they will not object (Article 97(6)).
